_comment: Guided tour for blind IRF estimation. Hand-built Qt (no view spec), so steps target toolbar actions by caption and the parameter spin boxes by the irf_* objectNames set in gui/tool.py. Read by chisurf.gui.widgets.tools.guided_tour.

steps.title: An IRF you did not measure
steps.text:
What you recorded is your molecule's decay convolved with the instrument's response to an infinitely short flash. Late in the record the response has long since ended, so the tail is the pure decay — fit it there and you know the decay without ever having seen the IRF. What connects the two is then recoverable by deconvolution.

That is what this does. It is a fallback, not a substitute for measuring the IRF, and the last step says why in detail.

Five steps.

steps.title: Load the decay
steps.text: From a file, or from a dataset already open in ChiSurf. It should be a decay whose tail is long enough to fit — the tail is the entire input to the first half of the method.

steps.title: Subtract the background before anything else
steps.text:
An offset that is not removed has no exponential shape to attribute to the decay — so the deconvolution attributes it to the IRF, as a long flat tail.

That is exactly what an instrument response cannot have, and exactly what will bias every lifetime you later fit with it. It is the most common way this method produces a confident, wrong answer.

Set the channel width from the acquisition too: everything downstream is in those units, and a wrong Δt gives a plausible IRF of the wrong width.

steps.title: Iterations are the regularisation, not a convergence setting
steps.text:
Richardson–Lucy does not converge to a sensible answer and stop. Left running, it converges to the noise — more iterations sharpen the estimate and amplify noise in the same motion, so where you stop is the regularisation.

Increase it until the IRF stops getting narrower in a way that looks structural, and no further. RL is used here because it keeps the result non-negative — which an IRF must be — and because it degrades gracefully instead of exploding on noisy data.

steps.title: Estimate — then distrust it in three specific ways
steps.text:
The tail is fitted, the IRF deconvolved, and both are plotted.

1. The circularity. An IRF estimated from a decay and then used to fit that same decay gives an excellent fit no matter what, because the IRF absorbed whatever the model could not describe. A good χ² here is not evidence. At minimum, fit a different measurement with it.
2. The tail fit is an assumption. It assumes one clean exponential. A multi-exponential sample, an unaccounted slow component, or a fit window that starts while the decay is still rising all transfer straight into the "IRF".
3. Does it look like an instrument response? One sharp peak, fast rise, short tail. Structure, a shoulder, or a width comparable to the lifetime you are measuring is a failed deconvolution — which will still convolve happily.

And if every lifetime you care about is far longer than the pulse, fit the tail directly instead: a method that needs no IRF beats one that invents one. The ? button has the rest.
